projects.title: Cyber risk assessment and risk register for a small company
projects.summary: Choose a small real organisation (a shop, an agency, an association), list its information assets, assess ten cyber risks with likelihood and impact, link each one to controls from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and present the top risks with a treatment plan.
projects.why: Every GRC role starts from the risk register. A clear, well-argued register for a real organisation shows recruiters the method they test in interviews: assets, threats, scoring, controls and decisions.

data.name: NIST SP 800-30: Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments
data.note: The reference method: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, impact.

data.name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
data.note: The functions and categories to map your controls to.

data.name: CIS Critical Security Controls
data.note: Concrete, prioritised controls for small organisations (implementation group 1).

steps.title: Choose the organisation and the scope
steps.text: Pick a small organisation you know. Describe in a few lines what it does, its people, its IT (laptops, e-mail, website, cloud tools, payment) and the scope of the assessment.

steps.title: List the assets
steps.text: List 10 to 15 information assets (customer file, accounting, website, e-mail, laptops…) with an owner and what matters most for each: confidentiality, integrity or availability.

steps.title: Define the scales
steps.text: Write a 1 to 4 scale for likelihood and one for impact, with a sentence for each level (for example impact 4 = activity stopped for more than a week or a breach of customer data).

steps.title: Assess ten risks
steps.text: For ten risks (phishing, ransomware, lost laptop, supplier outage, former employee still has access…), write the threat, the vulnerability, the impact, and score likelihood × impact.

steps.title: Map the controls
steps.text: For each risk, list the existing controls and the missing ones, mapped to a NIST CSF category and a CIS control, then score the residual risk.

steps.title: Decide the treatment
steps.text: Set a risk appetite (for example residual score above 8 must be treated). For each risk above it: reduce, transfer, avoid or accept, with an owner, a cost estimate and a date.

steps.title: Report
steps.text: Make a one-page summary for the manager: a heat map of the risks, the top five and the five actions to start with.

deliverables: The risk register (Excel or Google Sheets) with scales, scores and owners
A control mapping to NIST CSF and the CIS Controls
A one-page summary with a heat map and the five first actions
checklist: Each risk names an asset, a threat, a vulnerability and an impact
Likelihood and impact use written scales, not gut feeling
Inherent and residual scores are both shown
Every treated risk has an owner and a date
At least one risk is formally accepted, with the reason
No real confidential information from the organisation is published

cv.bullet: Carried out a cyber risk assessment for [organisation] (personal project): 12 assets, 10 risks scored on likelihood and impact, controls mapped to NIST CSF and CIS, and a prioritised treatment plan.
cv.talk: Explain how you chose the scales, the risk that surprised you most, and why you accepted one risk instead of treating it.

stretch: Repeat the assessment with the EBIOS Risk Manager method and compare the results.
Build the heat map in Power BI with a filter per owner.
Write the information security policy (two pages) that follows from your register.

projects.title: ISO 27001 gap assessment and Statement of Applicability
projects.summary: Compare a real or sample organisation with the 93 controls of ISO 27001 Annex A, write the Statement of Applicability, rate the maturity of each control and build the action plan to reach certification.
projects.why: The gap assessment is the first deliverable of almost every ISO 27001 project and a common task for junior GRC consultants. Doing one shows you know the standard in detail and can turn it into a realistic plan.

data.name: ISO/IEC 27001 (ISO)
data.note: The official page: scope of the standard and its structure.

data.name: Guide d’hygiène informatique (ANSSI)
data.note: 42 practical measures, in French, to check controls against.

data.name: CIS Critical Security Controls
data.note: Concrete technical controls to propose in the action plan.

steps.title: Define the organisation and scope
steps.text: Describe a real organisation you know well or a sample one (for example a 60-person software company with a SaaS product). Write the ISMS scope in two sentences.

steps.title: Build the control list
steps.text: In a sheet, list the Annex A controls by theme (organisational, people, physical, technological) with their numbers and short names, written in your own words.

steps.title: Rate the maturity
steps.text: For each control, write what exists today and rate it from 0 (nothing) to 4 (documented, applied and measured), with the evidence that would prove it.

steps.title: Write the Statement of Applicability
steps.text: Mark each control applicable or not, with the justification (a risk, a law, a contract), and its status.

steps.title: Check the management system
steps.text: Check clauses 4 to 10 too: scope, policy, roles, risk assessment, awareness, internal audit, management review. List what is missing.

steps.title: Build the action plan
steps.text: Group the gaps into 10 to 15 actions, each with an owner, an effort estimate, a priority and a quarter, up to a target certification date.

steps.title: Present it
steps.text: Make a short deck for management: overall maturity per theme, the main gaps, the plan and what it will need (people, tools, budget).

deliverables: The gap assessment sheet with maturity scores and expected evidence
A prioritised action plan to certification
checklist: All four Annex A themes are covered
Each maturity score has a written reason
Every excluded control has a justification
The management system clauses (4 to 10) are assessed, not only Annex A
Actions have an owner, a priority and a date
The text of the standard itself is not copied (it is copyrighted): controls are summarised in your own words

cv.bullet: Performed an ISO 27001:2022 gap assessment of [organisation] (personal project): 93 Annex A controls rated for maturity, Statement of Applicability and a 12-month action plan to certification.
cv.talk: Explain which theme was weakest and why, one control you excluded and how you justified it, and how you ordered the action plan.

stretch: Write two of the missing policies (access control, supplier security).
Map your controls to NIS2 obligations and show the overlap.
Turn the action plan into a Gantt chart with milestones up to the audit.

projects.title: GDPR record of processing and a data protection impact assessment
projects.summary: For a real or sample organisation, build the record of processing activities, choose the riskiest processing, carry out its data protection impact assessment (DPIA) and write the supplier and breach procedures that go with it.
projects.why: Personal data protection is part of most GRC roles in Europe. A clean record of processing and a complete DPIA show you can turn the regulation into concrete documents that an authority or an auditor would accept.

data.name: GDPR article 30: records of processing activities
GDPR article 35: data protection impact assessment
data.note: When a DPIA is required and what it covers.

data.name: CNIL PIA software
data.note: The French authority’s free tool to carry out a DPIA step by step.

steps.title: Choose the organisation
steps.text: Pick a real organisation you know (a gym, a training centre, an online shop) or a sample one, and list its departments and tools.

steps.title: Build the record
steps.text: List 8 to 12 processing activities (customers, payroll, recruitment, CCTV, newsletter…) with purpose, lawful basis, categories of data and people, recipients, transfers outside the EU, retention and security measures.

steps.title: Choose the DPIA
steps.text: Use the criteria of article 35 and the authority’s lists to find the processing that needs a DPIA (for example health data or large-scale monitoring) and explain why.

steps.title: Carry out the DPIA
steps.text: Describe the processing, check necessity and proportionality, assess the risks for the people (illegitimate access, unwanted change, disappearance of data) and the measures that reduce them.

steps.title: Review the processors
steps.text: For the two main suppliers that handle the data, check the data processing agreement, the hosting location and their security, using their public documents.

steps.title: Write the breach procedure
steps.text: One page: how a breach is detected and reported internally, who decides, how to notify the authority within 72 hours and when to inform the people.

deliverables: A complete DPIA for one processing
A one-page personal data breach procedure
checklist: Every processing has a lawful basis and a retention period
The DPIA choice is justified with the article 35 criteria
Risks are assessed for the people concerned, not only for the company
Transfers outside the EU are identified with their safeguard
The breach procedure names the 72-hour deadline and who decides
No real personal data is used in the deliverables

cv.bullet: Built the GDPR record of processing for [organisation] (personal project): 10 processing activities, a data protection impact assessment with the CNIL PIA method, two processor reviews and a 72-hour breach procedure.
cv.talk: Explain why that processing needed a DPIA, the main risk for the people concerned, and one measure you recommended.

stretch: Write the privacy notice that matches the record, in plain language.
Add the data subject rights procedure (access, erasure) with response templates.
Compare the record with what the organisation’s website says and list the differences.
